title: Saragarhi Day
hook: every 12 September the twenty-one are remembered

segments.voice: Yesterday, saka, and your line was the peaceful martyrs. Today's day of memory is about soldiers, and it's kept in a very different way.

The little post at Saragarhi talked to the world with a mirror and the sun: flashes of light sent from fort to fort across the ridge. Earlier on this path you heard how the signals kept coming the day the post was surrounded, and how the men inside stayed. Now the post is gone. What's left is a day on the calendar. On Saragarhi Day, in regimental halls, in gurdwaras and in homes, someone reads out a list of names, and people stand still while it's read.
screen: `A MIRROR AND THE SUN.` → `THE POST IS GONE.` → `A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: The story in one breath: Sikh soldiers of a British Indian regiment held a small signal post called Saragarhi, under Havildar Ishar Singh. A much larger force surrounded it. They held on, Sikh memory says, until the last of them had fallen. That memory counts them: twenty-one. The day is kept by name. The Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army marks Saragarhi Day, and so do Sikh gatherings far beyond it. A roll is read. Havildar Ishar Singh. The signaler, Gurmukh Singh. And the rest, one at a time. A number like twenty-one is easy to say and easy to forget. Names are harder to forget. Each name is a person who stayed. Sikhs often bring a verse to days like this. In a salok of Bhagat Kabir on Ang 1105, Kabir says, in paraphrase, that the true hero is the one who fights for the helpless, and who, though cut to pieces, never leaves the field. Some Sikh teachers read Kabir first as speaking of the inner battle, with one's own fear and greed. But his picture of someone who won't leave the field is why the salok is heard on a day like this. And the honest part: the men who attacked the post were fighting for their own valleys and homes. The day isn't kept against them. It's kept for twenty-one people, and for the plain fact that they stayed.
screen: `A SMALL POST, AND THEY STAYED.` · `THE DAY IS KEPT BY NAME.` · `KABIR: HE NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · `NOT KEPT AGAINST ANYONE.` · then, large: `TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand, feet planted, hands at your sides, and count slowly in your head to twenty-one, letting each count be one person; you don't need to know their names. Then sit down and let the breath steady itself. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them; if you don't, let the stillness be your way of honoring them.
Saragarhi Day. The day each year when the soldiers of the post at Saragarhi are remembered by name. Today's word.
Your line: twenty-one. Twenty-one names, read one at a time. That's day one thousand forty-eight.
